sentences.text: Barawertornis is an extinct genus of bird belonging to the family Dromornithidae, a group of flightless birds that lived from the Oligocene to the Miocene.
The only species in this genus is Barawertornis tedfordi, which was established by Patricia Vickers-Rich in 1979 based on fragmentary remains first reported by Richard H. Tedford.

Anatomical features such as a tibiotarsus shaft slightly curved from side to side and an external femoral condyle about one-third the width of the internal condyle suggest adaptations for a running lifestyle.

Other skeletal traits include a caudal intermuscular line present on most femurs but absent in specimen QM F30352, a distal vascular foramen found in Barawertornis tedfordi but missing in most Dromornis stirtoni specimens, and a mandible lacking a caudal mandibular fenestra.

The pterygoid possesses a dorsal process running above the quadrate articulation, a feature also seen in Dromornis planei, while the rostrum likely resembled that of Genyornis due to similarly slender and narrow mandibles.
Barawertornis tedfordi is the smallest known dromornithid species, with a weight estimated between 26.9 and 79 kg.
Fossil evidence reveals pathologies including unhealed bite marks, fractures, and gouges on a damaged tarsometatarsus attributed to predators, scavengers, or trampling.

Fragmentary remains of a dromornithid were first reported from the Carl Creek Limestone in Queensland in 1968 by Richard H. Tedford, leading Patricia Vickers-Rich to establish the genus and species Barawertornis tedfordi in 1979.
Skull material was later referred to Barawertornis in a 2016 study by Trevor Worthy and colleagues.
The genus name combines an Aboriginal word for 'ground' and the Ancient Greek word for 'bird', and it was originally assigned to the subfamily Barawertornithinae.
Barawertornis was likely a browser that ate leaves and fruit, similar to other dromornithids.
A 2024 study suggests that Barawertornis, like other dromornithids, may have had adaptations for an aquatic feeding style.

Pathologies, including unhealed bite marks and fractures, were reported in Barawertornis fossils by Nguyen et al. in 2010, and researchers hypothesize that these injuries on a femur were caused by a crocodilian predator like Baru.
Barawertornis lived during the Oligocene and Miocene epochs, specifically between 23.04 and 15.98 million years ago during the Aquitanian to Burdigalian stages.
Fossils found in Riversleigh, Queensland, indicate it inhabited Australia, where the Late Oligocene habitat consisted of open forests with sclerophyllous vegetation and deciduous vine thickets.

Fossils have also been reported from the Leaf Locality of the Wipajiri Formation in northern South Australia, though the age of this site is uncertain, with studies suggesting it dates to either the Early or Middle Miocene.
It is debated whether Barawertornis belongs to the Ilbandornis lineage, with some researchers suggesting similarities in the crania support this.
